LEGENDS FROM A NEGRO EDITOR
TALLADEGA, ALA. - It was about this time of year when we launched The Lighthouse And Informer in Charleston, back in 1939. It suspended publication from Columbia in 1954, having moved its offices from Charleston late in 1941.
About this same time of year, we begin preparations for the annual observance of Negro Newspaper Week. We used to have the observance during March, the month the first Negro Newspaper published in the United States began its circulation, March 16, 1827.
After The Lighthouse, I worked with The Afro- American Newspapers, The Pittsburgh Courier, The Chicago Defender and The Atlanta Daily World. moving from there in 1964 to Talladega College, retiring on October 1, 1981.
There is something about working on a newspaper that haunts you forever. It s more than the smell of printer s ink, the sight of it on your hands and dothing. It s more than writing a story, an editorial piece and helping them get into print. Whatever it is, say oldtimers in the profession, it gets into your blood. If you happen to be non-white and get into this business, you are definitely on a shoe string in resources, plagued by meeting payrolls, the rent, utilities and the various and sundry other expenses connected with the business hard-nosed business people say are so worrisome that only a plum stomped down fool would do what you are trying to do. Invariably, you are committed to fighting for an ethnic group that doesn t patronize you enough to pay even die rent. You have to find some way of trading enough with white concerns that will work with you, while you consistently blast away at some other whites. Sort of crazy business.
But, this is also the legend in part of that first Negro Newspaper, Freedom s Journal. Even in the free city of New York, it ran into money troubles with its very first issue. It was stirring up trouble between the races, critics said. It didn t reflect the attitude of the high and mighty free Negroes in New York, they cleared with the whitefolk. One of its founding editors, John Russwurm, quit within the first year, caught a boat for1 Liberia, and died over there as superintendent of education for the government. The desperate publishers of the newspaper changed its name in 1830 to The RIGHTS OF ALL. That didn t change things for it. ,
SOME 112 YEARS LATER
So, there we were, some 112 years later, launching yet another of the countless newspapers Negroes operated after Freedom s Journal. The faces and names out there had changed, but little else. And, each year since I left the field I get a sort of mysterious, funny feeling, almost hypnotic in its stories we broke, exposures of what we used to call snakes - Black and white who forever nibbled at the heels of a people God had assigned to the color of skins and textures of their hair. Strangely, looking back, we did have much fun and came to see and know heart break, racism, meanness and all the ugly things people inflict on people.
I wonder what became of the correspondent we had in a Pee Dee county who sent the story about a prominent Mullins citizen s funeral services. The story, done in long hand, began in these words: Funeral services for (name of the deceased) were hell in Mt. Olive Church Sunday afternoon We chuckled over the spelling but a bit later, funeral services for a Columbia txisinessman in Mt. Pisgah AME Church at Sumter, hometown of the deceased, were indeed just about the misspelled hell in the Mullins story: the girlfriend and two husky men bearing a huge Bleeding Heart floral, entered the church from the rear as services just began and, the woman leading all dressed in pretty black, marched slowly up the aisle where the floral was erected in front of the casket. What the wife said and did we didn t think should have been published. So, we didn t.
From its beginning, staff people on The Lighthouse were fiercely dedicated - down to the carriers and folk who sold copies weekly. We will always remember those on the first edition: W. Eugene Simmons, columnist, Wm. H. Simmons, Sr. (no relatiion), advertising space sales, Augustus Campbell, circulation, Julian (Smoke) Walker, sports, Mrs. Eva Hunt Hopkins, society and, Cornelius Glover, photography.
A firm, always encouraging supporter was D. Ireland Thomas, manager of the Lincoln Theatre on King Street. Mr. Thomas also had stock in the Bijou chain, operating out of Nashville, TN. By the way, it was he who donated the site on Coming Street to which the old John Street City Fire Station, a Black unit, was transferred. And, there were the so many times the Reverend Dr. Jesse E. Beard of the AME Church went out of his way to keep spirits up.
The same can be said of Funeral Director Peter Johnson of Mt. Pleasant, the Reverend Norridge B. Mayham of Georgetown in those early years. People like Rev. J.P. Waring, Rev. B.J. Whipper, Rev. J.C. James, Sam Faber, Andy McCottry, Reverend Louis Simmons, Frank McKenzie and there were Mr. and Mrs. Edward Taylor of Taylor s Bakery. C.A. could be heard over much of Black Charleston Sunday mornings. He was consistently the largest handler of street sales.

Pressure from the city came down after we headlined Whites Frame Doctor; Force Him From Town. It was an account from Dr. William (Billy) Felder of how he was saved from a mob of whites awaiting his return on a Saturday morning to McClellanville. A widely circulated statement about the NAACP, which has been promoted actively by anti-Negro elements of the South, is that its policy is charted by a handful of northerners, mostly New Yorkers, who have taken it upon themselves to dictate to the rest of the nation concerning rights for Negroes. Actually, Association policy is formulated by the body s annual convention, a representative group of some one thousand NAACP members from all sections of the United States and Alaska. The policy set by the convention is carried out by the Board of Directors of forty-eight members which also selects the executive secretary, who, in turn, appoints the staff.
The present Board of Directors, of whom about seventy-five per cent are Negroes, has more than thirty-three per cent Southerners in its ranks, including persons from Louisiana, Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia. Among current board members are the Rt. Rev. Stephen Gill Spottswood, Walter Reuther, Ralph J. Bunche, Mrs. Eleanor Roosevelt, Rev. Benjamin E. Mays, Herbert H. Lehman, Judge William H. Hastie, Mrs. Jessie M. Vann. The interests of board members, in addition to those of the several named above, include civic leader, business executive, physician, attorney, and homemaker. Members of the Board are elected for three-year terms; one-third of the Board is elected each year by means of a referendum among branches.
The Association s staff, headed by Roy Wilkins, executive secretary, includes the noted civil rights attorney, Thurgood Marshall, and such other department heads as Clarence Mitchell, director of the Washington Bureau; Gloster B. Current, director of branches; Herbert Hill, labor secretary; Madison S. Jones, special assistant for housing; John Morsell, assistant to the executive secretary; James Ivy, editor of The Crisis, the Association s monthly organ; and Henry Lee Moon, director of public relations. A church secretary is scheduled for early appointment.
Notes on History
The formation of the Association, perhaps ironically, was immediately influenced by an incident in the' North. In the words of Mary White Ovington, a white social worker who was a founder of the NAACP:
In the summer of 1908, the country was shocked by the account of the race riots at Springfield, Illinois. Here, in the home of Abraham Lincoln, a mob containing many of the town s best citizens, raged for two days, killed and wounded scores of Negroes, and drove thousands from the city. Articles on the subject appeared in newspapers and magazines. Among them was one in The Independent of September 3, by William English Walling, entitled Race War in the North. After describing the atrocities committed against the colored people, Mr. Walling declared :
Either the spirit of the abolitionists, of Lincoln and of Lovejoy must be revived and we must come to treat the Negro on a plane of absolute political and social equality, or Vardaman and Tillman will soon have transferred the race war to the North.
In January, 1909, Miss Ovington relates, she met with Mr. Walling and Dr. Henry Moskowitz and the three selected February 12, Lincoln s birthday, for the issuance of a call for a national conference on the Negro question.
The Lincoln s birthday call, Miss Ovington continues, was drafted by Oswald Garrison Villard, then president of the New York Evening Post Company, and said in part:
If Mr. Lincoln could revisit this country in the flesh, he would be disheartened and discouraged. . . . The spread of lawless attacks upon the Negro, North, South, and West even in the Springfield made famous by Lincoln often accompanied by revolting brutalities, sparing neither sex nor age nor youth, could but shock the author of the sentiment that government of the people, by the people, and for the people, shall not perish from the earth. Silence under these conditions means tacit approval. . . . Hence, we call upon all the believers in democracy to join in a national conference for the discussion of present evils, the voicing of protests, and the renewal of the struggle for civil and political liberty.
Among the fifty-three signers of this call were Jane Addams, John Dewey, John L. Elliott, William Lloyd Garrison, Rev. Francis J. Grimke, Rabbi Emil G. Hirsch, Rev. John Haynes Holmes, Rev. Frederick Lynch, Rev. Charles H. Parkhurst, J. G. Phelps Stokes, Lincoln Steffens, Rabbi Stephen S. Wise, Bishop Alexander Walters, William English Walling, and Lillian D. Wald.
To continue in the words of Miss Ovington: We have had five conferences since 1909 [her account was written in 1914], but I doubt whether any have been so full of a questioning surprise, amounting swiftly to enthusiasm, on the part of the white people in attendance. These men and women, engaged in religious, social, and educational work, for the first time met the Negro who demands, not a pittance, but his full rights in the commonwealth. . . . In May, 1910, we held our second conference in New York, and again our meetings were attended by earnest, interested people. It was then that we organized a permanent body to be known as the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People . . . pledged to a nation-wide work for justice to the Negro race.
One Broad Accomplishment
In 1957, surveying nearly a half-century of NAACP work, the outstanding over-all accomplishment of the organization, in the opinion of its leaders, might be said to be a general loosening of the color-caste system of the United States. The system, though still operative, is declared to have lost a degree of its former inflexibility.
Robert Morrison Maclver, a well-known sociologist, set forth the results of a study of intergroup discrimination in the United States in a book, The More Perfect Union (New York, Macmillan, 1948), in which he stated:
It is beyond contention that in the United States all colored people and this designation must here be extended to include Chinese, Hindus, Japanese, Koreans, and Filipinos, as well as Negroes, and for fuller measure American Indians and Latin Americans are commonly regarded as and commonly treated as constituting a lower caste. In the drawing of this line practically no distinction is made between people of high cultural achievement

Lynching
Until recent years, a concomitant of the caste subordination of Negroes was the lynching by mobs, which often carried on this macabre activity secure in the knowledge that predominant local sentiment was on their side. Statistics cited by Walter White, late executive secretary of the NAACP, in his book, Rope and Faggot: A Biography of Judge Lynch (New York, Knopf, 1929), show that during the two decades 1890 to 1910, mobs lynched 2,586 men and women, while in the years 1910 to 1927, the lynchers claimed 1,144 victims. As Garrison, in The Liberator, relentlessly held up the horrors of chattel slavery to the world, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People relentlessly broadcasted this [lynching] and other stories of the horrors perpetrated against the black man. One hun- dred-page study [Thirty Years of Lynching in the United States, 1890-1918] went to libraries, not only in this country but throughout the world. . . . Besides the publicity of the printed word, we used the public meeting. ...
The NAACP also campaigned persistently for a federal anti-lynching law and although such legislation never became a reality, the campaign itself served as an education for many white Americans by further exposing the extent and the horrors of lynching.
Walter White s Observations
The analysis of the causes of lynching to which most of Mr. White s book, Rope and Faggot, is devoted, probably had an effect upon those who read the volume, published in 1929. A chapter dealing with the relationship between expressions of Christianity and lynching, for example, states in part:

The Association s activities in this regard have made a part of recent American history. Elsewhere today as has happened throughout history repressed minorities are seeking redress of grievances by torch, dagger and bomb, instruments that produce social chaos and involve loss of precious moral values. . . . privilege surrendered of its own accord. Nor will it If to go slow is to relax pressures through the courts and public opinion, no social change will be effected.
Hiring a Lawyer
By hiring a good lawyer and going to court, as Mr. Barnett puts it, the NAACP has won a long list of favorable legal decisions. The Association reports that it has won forty-two of forty-six cases it carried to the United States Supreme Court. Among these Supreme Court decisions are those declaring segregation unconstitutional in public elementary and secondary schools, public colleges and universities, public parks and playgrounds, interstate travel vehicles, and intrastate buses. The judicial enforcement of racially restrictive covenants in housing has been invalidated by the Supreme Court, as has been the denial of jury duty to Negroes and varied maneuvers to prevent Negroes from voting. The right of an accused person to a trial in an atmosphere not dominated by the mob also has been established by the court.

Supreme Court resulted in a decision, November 13, 1956, that the enforced racial separation of local bus passengers in Alabama is unconstitutional.

One of the widely discussed organizations in the United States is the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, with headquarters at 20 West 40th Street, New York 18, N. Y. Nearly two hundred years after the adoption of the Declaration of Independence, proclaiming that all men are created equal, the American social scene of midTwentieth Century is marked by a turbulent struggle between those striving toward basic human rights for all Americans and those who oppose such rights. Generally considered as one of the leaders of the former forces is the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, which has as its goal the establishment of equal rights for citizens of all races and religions with respect to: security of the person, housing, education, employment, voting, and various public accommodations.
Three-fold Approach
In working to achieve its goal, the NAACP makes a three-fold attack on racial discrimination: legal, legislative, and educational. In brief, the NAACP plan of action consists of court tests, espousal of anti-discrimination laws, and a public information program.
The NAACP does not propose to await the enlightenment of all members of a given locality before proceeding with positive work to bring about equality of citizenship rights in the area. This view of the Association received unsolicited support in a recent article summarizing public opinion surveys conducted throughout the United States during the past fourteen years by the National Opinion Research Center at the University of Chicago, which concluded that it is not necessary to wait until a majority of whites are ready, to grant the Negro equal access to schools, buses, and residential neighborhoods.

The NAACP is a large membership organization, with some 350,000 members located in almost every state, the District of Columbia, and Alaska. May 19, 1984
South Carolina
The Way It Was
By John H. McCray
NEGRO SOUTH SHOULD ORGANIZE
TALLADEGA, ALA. -- In response to a call initiated by the South Carolina Progressive Democrats, representatives from 11 southern states met in the Butler Street YMCA in Atlanta and, among other things organized the Southern Democratic Conference. Elected chairman was Judge A.T. Walden of Atlanta; vice chairman was his writer, then living at Columbia, S.C. Several Others from South Carolina were also elected to offices or committees. The meeting was held the first week in June, 1962; it recessed to a second meeting in Birmingham, held in September, 1962.
Both 1962 meetings dealt with speeding up action on several commitments the Democratic National Committee had made in February 1961. The party had agreed to come up with means by which Negroes would be registered to vote in the south without harassment and subterfuges from local registration board people, often abetted by the sheriff s department and other petty satraps that were part of the courthouse gang. The new help included getting the people to and from the courthouse to register, and to and from voting precincts on election day. That the Negro South wanted these things instead of the few low totem pole jobs patronage offered. John F. Kennedy had won the 1960 presidential election only with the vote, mostly solid in the south, from Negro voters. In South Carolina, Negroes had turned down patronage offers of the Truman administration when he was continued as president in 1948. Two years later, they had also rejected patronage slots from incumbent U.S. Senator Olin D. Johnson, who narrowly defeated former Governor J. Strom Thurmond. The only thing new then in 1961 in the request filed with the Democratic National Committee was it now included 11 states - instead of only South Carolina.
One of the most vibrant persons in the June 1962 organizational meeting was YMCA Secretary Warren Cochrane, a native of Charleston. It is interesting to recall that some 22 years later, what both Mr. Cochrane and Georgia s first post-Reconstruction Black senator- to-be, Attorney LeRoy Johnson, argued is very much a reality in 1984: they urged for programs within the new Democratic (Southern) Conference that insured against Negroes in the 11 member states being exploited by persons of their own ethnic group living outside the south. It was a heated meeting and recessed - not adjourned - to a September meeting in Birmingham.
SOME THINK AREA PEOPLE DUMB
The National Committee sent down from Washington Deputy Chairman Louis E. Martin and White House staffer Andrew Hatcher for the June 1962 meeting. The Deputy Chairman reported funds had been contributed by a foundation to launch registration. The money had been allocated among three groups, NAACP, Southern Regional Council and the fledgling SCLC. No contact nor consultation with the leaders who actually had the voters had been made prior to the session. The delegates did not object to NAACP s involvement; however, they were virtually acrimoniously bitter about SRC and SCLC.
Mr. Martin privately explained later the individual state leaders had been by-passed and the funds turned over to the three organizations as the only handling since the foundation providing the funds had to steer clear of partisan political involvement - an IRS requirement. Nevertheless, the 11 state leaders were the people who rounded up and gotten out the votes Mr. Kennedy won with, doing so out of their own pockets, or money their organizations raised from among Negroes themselves.
THE KENNEDYS GOT WISE
Mr. Kennedy s campaign in 1960 was run by a committee that included about six Negroes in key spots. The six lived in, and north of, Washington, D.C., Marjorie Mackenzie Lawson apparently the most influential. Robert F. Kennedy, the candidate s brother, ran the campaign and indications were to turn up that he had been led to believe the six Blacks referred to were the nation s Negro brokers; that the rank and file Negro would follow them blindly. Consequently, RFK wasn t concerned about bitterness from, say the leaders in the 11 states, and that of then present Black Democrat, Rep. William L. Dawson, of Chicago. This was a New Frontiers campaign, and as literal as the words implied - younger and more sophisticated people, including six hand-picked Blacks. By August, Bobby Kennedy and the New Frontier people were stunned. The six people they d picked really didn t have the influence, impact and pull at first thought. But RFK et al did a fast about face. They feld to Dawson, apologized and urged him to help save the November election for the party. And to whom did Dawson turned? To the small 11 state leaders who established the Southern Democratic Conference two years later.
In recent months, the southern area - the same 11 states - have been the spots where several out-of-the- south people have been cavorting. Negro voters in this area, inspite of what one reads and hears or sees via media reports, have increased only because of efforts of local people living and working among them. These local people are given no recognition or credit today, just as none was given those ahead of them 22 years ago. We ve even had instances this year where outsiders have come into the area and attempted to discredit our own people who dare to think for themselves, who have been elected by people in their communities and insist on serving their communities rather than hand over everything they have built up to outsiders whose principle interest is self-deification and patronage and money.
The Southern Democratic Conference was intended to deal with things like what we re talking about. In 1962 and around that time they were kept out of, say South Carolina, and some other states. The reasoning then was if the Negro in the South is to become free, he must do it mostly himself. All he can get from most Negroes outside the area is a lot of mouth, a lot of collection plates - both before him and before others who are told he will benefit from the collections. A recounting of changes in the lifestyle of the south indisputably shows the southern Negro had had the courage, the determination and ability to organize his community behind goals he sets. He doesn t get, and really doesn t need, outside help. That is exactly what William Patterson proposed to S.C. Progressive Democrats in 1944. Aw, he beamed, they had done a marvelous, unbelievable thing. But they needed to have outside help which, in that case, was being offered by Communists. Asked where had he and his people been all the years Negro South Carolinians had wallowed in misery and deprivation? The man flushed in anger, swearing and accusing the party of being blankety blank nationalists.
When a definition of the word was learned a few days later, one of us said, He s damned right. We re more concerned about us in South Carolina.

It was then that we organized a permanent body to be known as the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People . . . pledged to a nation-wide work for justice to the Negro race.
One Broad Accomplishment
In 1957, surveying nearly a half-century of NAACP work, the outstanding over-all accomplishment of the organization, in the opinion of its leaders, might be said to be a general loosening of the color-caste system of the United States. The system, though still operative, is declared to have lost a degree of its former inflexibility.
Robert Morrison Maclver, a well-known sociologist, set forth the results of a study of intergroup discrimination in the United States in a book, The More Perfect Union (New York, Macmillan, 1948), in which he stated:

In the drawing of this line practically no distinction is made between people of high cultural achievement

or historical eminence and those which have no such pretensions.

Until recent years, a concomitant of the caste subordination of Negroes was the lynching by mobs, which often carried on this macabre activity secure in the knowledge that predominant local sentiment was on their side. Statistics cited by Walter White, late executive secretary of the NAACP, in his book, Rope and Faggot: A Biography of Judge Lynch (New York, Knopf, 1929), show that during the two decades 1890 to 1910, mobs lynched 2,586 men and women, while in the years 1910 to 1927, the lynchers claimed 1,144 victims. Besides the publicity of the printed word, we used the public meeting. ...

The analysis of the causes of lynching to which most of Mr. White s book, Rope and Faggot, is devoted, probably had an effect upon those who read the volume, published in 1929. A chapter dealing with the relationship between expressions of Christianity and lynching, for example, states in part:

Elsewhere today as has happened throughout history repressed minorities are seeking redress of grievances by torch, dagger and bomb, instruments that produce social chaos and involve loss of precious moral values. . . . privilege surrendered of its own accord. Nor will it If to go slow is to relax pressures through the courts and public opinion, no social change will be effected.

By hiring a good lawyer and going to court, as Mr. Barnett puts it, the NAACP has won a long list of favorable legal decisions. The Association reports that it has won forty-two of forty-six cases it carried to the United States Supreme Court. Among these Supreme Court decisions are those declaring segregation unconstitutional in public elementary and secondary schools, public colleges and universities, public parks and playgrounds, interstate travel vehicles, and intrastate buses. (Ed s Note: The first Black newspaper published in the South was The Colored American out of Augusta, Ga. Since that time in 1837, numerous publications have surfaced in the struggle for freedom, most notably The Lighthouse And Informer, published by Mr. John H. McCray, back in 1939, here in Charleston. As we approach the annual observance of Black Press Month nationwide during March, Mr. McCray will write a series of columns recalling his struggles, triumphs and reflections of Charleston in days past. The following is the first in a series.)
LEGENDS FROM A NEGRO EDITOR
TALLADEGA, ALA. - It was about this time of year when we launched The Lighthouse And Informer in Charleston, back in 1939. It suspended publication from Columbia in 1954, having moved its offices from Charleston late in 1941.
About this same time of year, we begin preparations for the annual observance of Negro Newspaper Week. We used to have the observance during March, the month the first Negro Newspaper published in the United States began its circulation, March 16, 1827.
After The Lighthouse, I worked with The Afro- American Newspapers, The Pittsburgh Courier, The Chicago Defender and The Atlanta Daily World. moving from there in 1964 to Talladega College, retiring on October 1, 1981.
There is something about working on a newspaper that haunts you forever. It s more than the smell of printer s ink, the sight of it on your hands and dothing. It s more than writing a story, an editorial piece and helping them get into print. Whatever it is, say oldtimers in the profession, it gets into your blood. If you happen to be non-white and get into this business, you are definitely on a shoe string in resources, plagued by meeting payrolls, the rent, utilities and the various and sundry other expenses connected with the business hard-nosed business people say are so worrisome that only a plum stomped down fool would do what you are trying to do. Invariably, you are committed to fighting for an ethnic group that doesn t patronize you enough to pay even die rent. You have to find some way of trading enough with white concerns that will work with you, while you consistently blast away at some other whites. Sort of crazy business.
But, this is also the legend in part of that first Negro Newspaper, Freedom s Journal. Even in the free city of New York, it ran into money troubles with its very first issue. It was stirring up trouble between the races, critics said. It didn t reflect the attitude of the high and mighty free Negroes in New York, they cleared with the whitefolk. One of its founding editors, John Russwurm, quit within the first year, caught a boat for1 Liberia, and died over there as superintendent of education for the government. The desperate publishers of the newspaper changed its name in 1830 to The RIGHTS OF ALL. That didn t change things for it. ,
SOME 112 YEARS LATER
So, there we were, some 112 years later, launching yet another of the countless newspapers Negroes operated after Freedom s Journal. The faces and names out there had changed, but little else. And, each year since I left the field I get a sort of mysterious, funny feeling, almost hypnotic in its stories we broke, exposures of what we used to call snakes - Black and white who forever nibbled at the heels of a people God had assigned to the color of skins and textures of their hair. Strangely, looking back, we did have much fun and came to see and know heart break, racism, meanness and all the ugly things people inflict on people.
I wonder what became of the correspondent we had in a Pee Dee county who sent the story about a prominent Mullins citizen s funeral services. The story, done in long hand, began in these words: Funeral services for (name of the deceased) were hell in Mt. Olive Church Sunday afternoon We chuckled over the spelling but a bit later, funeral services for a Columbia txisinessman in Mt. Pisgah AME Church at Sumter, hometown of the deceased, were indeed just about the misspelled hell in the Mullins story: the girlfriend and two husky men bearing a huge Bleeding Heart floral, entered the church from the rear as services just began and, the woman leading all dressed in pretty black, marched slowly up the aisle where the floral was erected in front of the casket. What the wife said and did we didn t think should have been published. So, we didn t.

TALLADEGA, ALA. -- Watching the Tony Down s Journal on TV, shown in this area on Sunday, I shuddered when NAACP executive director Ben Hooks of the organization being featured remarked something like The NAACP is the greatest thing Hack people have accomplished in this century.
In addition to being executive director, Ben Hooks is an attorney and a minister. He certainly must have read the history of his organization and knows from that, and from day to day operations, that NAACP came into existence under a merger of two groups: the National Negro Committee, a group of whites led by southerner William English Walling, reporter for the N.Y. Evening Post Mary White Ovington, and Dr. Henry Moskowitz, a social worker. They met and organized in New York City on February 12, 1909 on the 100th birthday anniversary of President Abraham Lincoln. This National Negro Committee merged later with the Niagara Movement, founded by some 29 Negro intellectuals Dr. W.E.B. DuBois got together at Buffalo, July 11-13, 1905. The thrust at the Buffalo inhering was a denunication of Booker T.
Washington s celebrated Atlanta Compromise $>eech of 1895. DuBois was a professor at Atlanta University at the time. He took strong exceptions to this portion of the speech, It is important and right that all privileges of the law be ours, but it is vastly more important that we be prepared for the exercise of those privileges. DuBois favored pressing for civil rights, and had led protest gatherings in several American cities to under-score his position. He was made editor of the merged organization s publication, The Crisis, the first edition having borne the November 1910 date.
SUPPORTED LARGELY BY WHITES
Its present name was adopted after the merger. Most of its financial support has always came from white sources and resources, and continues that way nearly 73 years after the founding. Early in the 1950s, I met with Thurgood Marshall, at the time head of its legal staff, a Sunday afternoon in his office at the old NAACP headquarters in New York City. The conference was to have an indepth understanding of his resources, and such as we had in South Carolina at the time, for legal cases such as the history making Clarendon County school desegregation case, and another also history making case - Sarah Mae Flemming s city bus suit against S.C. Electric and Gas at Columbia, the model for the Rosa Parks case at Montgomery, Ala. some two years after Miss Flemming s.
I won t forget how Thurgood finally stoop up, walked around his desk to a large window and stood quietly looking over the terrain stories below his office. Come here, John, he said quietly. He pointed to directions he said were Harlem, to Brooklyn and some others. There are over 1,000,000 (a million) Negroes living in those boroughs. We don t have 500 NAACP members there now in the whole New York area. South Carolina at the time had over 110 NAACP chapters, several of them with more paid memberships than all of the N.Y. Negro-dominated sections of town. He said it was no better most other larger, and presumedly freer, places around the country. Membership fees were $1 each, per year, at that time.
The organization says now it has over 500,000 paid memberships, largest of any of the civil rights organizations. Some of these are white members. Its main source of income is from foundations, wealthy whites and some special contributions from a few Black groups. There is no question, however, but that ftie reason NAACP exists is it has been paid for by whites. So, Ben Hooks errors inexcusably when he attempts to credit Negroes with having done something so good to help themselves while, in reality, most of them have cared less.
Thurgood Marshall often expressed an indebtedness to white sources for rationales on which NAACP cases were built. Two examples: it was Columbia University Law School students who gave him the key he used to short circuit South Carolina s Olin D. Johnston s (governor) to keep the primaries white. Judge J. It was he who telephoned Thurgood one night from Charleston and instructed him to prepare an amended complaint in the pending case before Mr. Waring from Garendon County. The pending case sought remedy under the old Plessy vs Ferguson Separate but Equal rationale that Mr. Waring said had never worked, wasn t working then, and would never work. Even the NAACP executive secretary, the late Walter White, was to confess later that while the Waring handling of the Clarendon suit was a happy, startling surprise, it was something he himself had never so mich as dared to hope for.
WHY NOT JUST TELL IT LIKE IT IS?
It was a small, likely unthinking mistake Ben Hooks made; but it is also made everywhere by Negroes rais- hg money for schools and colleges, churches, rounding up money for their businesses and professions, for employment and other things on an unending list. Among the Association s twenty-one vice-presidents those who perhaps are best known in their respective fields are Norman Cousins, Oscar Hammerstein II, Rev. John Haynes Holmes, Wayne Morse, Bishop W. J. Walls, Rabbi Judah Cahn, Rev. William Lloyd Imes, Eric Johnston, and A. Philip Randolph.
A widely circulated statement about the NAACP, which has been promoted actively by anti-Negro elements of the South, is that its policy is charted by a handful of northerners, mostly New Yorkers, who have taken it upon themselves to dictate to the rest of the nation concerning rights for Negroes. Actually, Association policy is formulated by the body s annual convention, a representative group of some one thousand NAACP members from all sections of the United States and Alaska. The policy set by the convention is carried out by the Board of Directors of forty-eight members which also selects the executive secretary, who, in turn, appoints the staff.
The present Board of Directors, of whom about seventy-five per cent are Negroes, has more than thirty-three per cent Southerners in its ranks, including persons from Louisiana, Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia. Among current board members are the Rt. Rev. Stephen Gill Spottswood, Walter Reuther, Ralph J. Bunche, Mrs. Eleanor Roosevelt, Rev. Benjamin E. Mays, Herbert H. Lehman, Judge William H. Hastie, Mrs. Jessie M. Vann. The interests of board members, in addition to those of the several named above, include civic leader, business executive, physician, attorney, and homemaker. Members of the Board are elected for three-year terms; one-third of the Board is elected each year by means of a referendum among branches.
The Association s staff, headed by Roy Wilkins, executive secretary, includes the noted civil rights attorney, Thurgood Marshall, and such other department heads as Clarence Mitchell, director of the Washington Bureau; Gloster B. Current, director of branches; Herbert Hill, labor secretary; Madison S. Jones, special assistant for housing; John Morsell, assistant to the executive secretary; James Ivy, editor of The Crisis, the Association s monthly organ; and Henry Lee Moon, director of public relations. A church secretary is scheduled for early appointment.
Notes on History
The formation of the Association, perhaps ironically, was immediately influenced by an incident in the' North. In the words of Mary White Ovington, a white social worker who was a founder of the NAACP:
In the summer of 1908, the country was shocked by the account of the race riots at Springfield, Illinois. Here, in the home of Abraham Lincoln, a mob containing many of the town s best citizens, raged for two days, killed and wounded scores of Negroes, and drove thousands from the city. Articles on the subject appeared in newspapers and magazines. Among them was one in The Independent of September 3, by William English Walling, entitled Race War in the North. After describing the atrocities committed against the colored people, Mr. Walling declared :
Either the spirit of the abolitionists, of Lincoln and of Lovejoy must be revived and we must come to treat the Negro on a plane of absolute political and social equality, or Vardaman and Tillman will soon have transferred the race war to the North.
In January, 1909, Miss Ovington relates, she met with Mr. Walling and Dr. Henry Moskowitz and the three selected February 12, Lincoln s birthday, for the issuance of a call for a national conference on the Negro question.
The Lincoln s birthday call, Miss Ovington continues, was drafted by Oswald Garrison Villard, then president of the New York Evening Post Company, and said in part:
If Mr. Lincoln could revisit this country in the flesh, he would be disheartened and discouraged. . . . The spread of lawless attacks upon the Negro, North, South, and West even in the Springfield made famous by Lincoln often accompanied by revolting brutalities, sparing neither sex nor age nor youth, could but shock the author of the sentiment that government of the people, by the people, and for the people, shall not perish from the earth. Silence under these conditions means tacit approval. . . . Hence, we call upon all the believers in democracy to join in a national conference for the discussion of present evils, the voicing of protests, and the renewal of the struggle for civil and political liberty.
Among the fifty-three signers of this call were Jane Addams, John Dewey, John L. Elliott, William Lloyd Garrison, Rev. Francis J. Grimke, Rabbi Emil G. Hirsch, Rev. John Haynes Holmes, Rev. Frederick Lynch, Rev. Charles H. Parkhurst, J. G. Phelps Stokes, Lincoln Steffens, Rabbi Stephen S. Wise, Bishop Alexander Walters, William English Walling, and Lillian D. Wald.
To continue in the words of Miss Ovington: We have had five conferences since 1909 [her account was written in 1914], but I doubt whether any have been so full of a questioning surprise, amounting swiftly to enthusiasm, on the part of the white people in attendance. These men and women, engaged in religious, social, and educational work, for the first time met the Negro who demands, not a pittance, but his full rights in the commonwealth. . . . In May, 1910, we held our second conference in New York, and again our meetings were attended by earnest, interested people. It was then that we organized a permanent body to be known as the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People . . . pledged to a nation-wide work for justice to the Negro race.
One Broad Accomplishment
In 1957, surveying nearly a half-century of NAACP work, the outstanding over-all accomplishment of the organization, in the opinion of its leaders, might be said to be a general loosening of the color-caste system of the United States. The system, though still operative, is declared to have lost a degree of its former inflexibility.
Robert Morrison Maclver, a well-known sociologist, set forth the results of a study of intergroup discrimination in the United States in a book, The More Perfect Union (New York, Macmillan, 1948), in which he stated:
It is beyond contention that in the United States all colored people and this designation must here be extended to include Chinese, Hindus, Japanese, Koreans, and Filipinos, as well as Negroes, and for fuller measure American Indians and Latin Americans are commonly regarded as and commonly treated as constituting a lower caste. In the drawing of this line practically no distinction is made between people of high cultural achievement

Lynching
Until recent years, a concomitant of the caste subordination of Negroes was the lynching by mobs, which often carried on this macabre activity secure in the knowledge that predominant local sentiment was on their side. Statistics cited by Walter White, late executive secretary of the NAACP, in his book, Rope and Faggot: A Biography of Judge Lynch (New York, Knopf, 1929), show that during the two decades 1890 to 1910, mobs lynched 2,586 men and women, while in the years 1910 to 1927, the lynchers claimed 1,144 victims. Of these 3,730 persons who suffered the effect of mob sadism, a small number were white. Miss Ovington tells the story in her book, The Walls Come Tumbling Down (New York, Harcourt, 1947) :

One hun- dred-page study [Thirty Years of Lynching in the United States, 1890-1918] went to libraries, not only in this country but throughout the world. . . . Besides the publicity of the printed word, we used the public meeting. ...
The NAACP also campaigned persistently for a federal anti-lynching law and although such legislation never became a reality, the campaign itself served as an education for many white Americans by further exposing the extent and the horrors of lynching.
Walter White s Observations
The analysis of the causes of lynching to which most of Mr. White s book, Rope and Faggot, is devoted, probably had an effect upon those who read the volume, published in 1929. A chapter dealing with the relationship between expressions of Christianity and lynching, for example, states in part:

Protestantism in the lynching states has become the stronghold of bigotry, directing its onslaughts against Negroes, Catholics, and Jews.

The Association s activities in this regard have made a part of recent American history. Albert E. Barnett said in this letter:

Elsewhere today as has happened throughout history repressed minorities are seeking redress of grievances by torch, dagger and bomb, instruments that produce social chaos and involve loss of precious moral values. . . . The NAACP counsels patience and moderation, and admirably illustrates both. It hires a good lawyer and takes its cases to court.
Mr. Barnett s letter also points out: In no case has
privilege surrendered of its own accord. Nor will it If to go slow is to relax pressures through the courts and public opinion, no social change will be effected.
Hiring a Lawyer
By hiring a good lawyer and going to court, as Mr. Barnett puts it, the NAACP has won a long list of favorable legal decisions. The Association reports that it has won forty-two of forty-six cases it carried to the United States Supreme Court. Among these Supreme Court decisions are those declaring segregation unconstitutional in public elementary and secondary schools, public colleges and universities, public parks and playgrounds, interstate travel vehicles, and intrastate buses. The judicial enforcement of racially restrictive covenants in housing has been invalidated by the Supreme Court, as has been the denial of jury duty to Negroes and varied maneuvers to prevent Negroes from voting. The right of an accused person to a trial in an atmosphere not dominated by the mob also has been established by the court.
NAACP lawyers recently secured from the Interstate Commerce Commission a ruling that interstate passengers cannot be required to use segregated seating on carriers nor to use segregated waiting rooms. The year-long mass protest against racial discrimination on the city buses of Montgomery, Alabama, came to a successful conclusion when an NAACP case carried to the U. S. Supreme Court resulted in a decision, November 13, 1956, that the enforced racial separation of local bus passengers in Alabama is unconstitutional.
On the federal level, the Association has been unable to obtain passage of any civil rights legislation by Congress, such as that to make lynching a federal offense, to protect the right to vote, to ban racial discrimination in hospitals, employment, and housing. The NAACP has, however, been a factor in the passage of fair employment practices laws in fifteen states. On the subject of racial bias in employment, an NAACP leaflet declares:
Denying a man a decent job because of his race is denying him the basis of his existence. . . . The NAACP believes that an FEPC to guarantee citizens an opportunity to secure jobs on the basis of merit, not color or religion is the keystone of the federal civil rights program.
The NAACP also was successful in its efforts to secure enactment of anti-discrimination laws governing public housing and urban renewal in New York, Connecticut, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. New York State went further in 1955 when two laws, the first of their kind in the United States, were enacted banning racial discrimination in housing which has received publicly-insured or guaranteed financing from the Federal Housing Authority or the Veterans Administration.

South Carolina
The Way It Was

NEGRO SOUTH SHOULD ORGANIZE
TALLADEGA, ALA. -- In response to a call initiated by the South Carolina Progressive Democrats, representatives from 11 southern states met in the Butler Street YMCA in Atlanta and, among other things organized the Southern Democratic Conference. Elected chairman was Judge A.T. Walden of Atlanta; vice chairman was his writer, then living at Columbia, S.C. Several Others from South Carolina were also elected to offices or committees. The meeting was held the first week in June, 1962; it recessed to a second meeting in Birmingham, held in September, 1962.
Both 1962 meetings dealt with speeding up action on several commitments the Democratic National Committee had made in February 1961. The party had agreed to come up with means by which Negroes would be registered to vote in the south without harassment and subterfuges from local registration board people, often abetted by the sheriff s department and other petty satraps that were part of the courthouse gang. The new help included getting the people to and from the courthouse to register, and to and from voting precincts on election day. That the Negro South wanted these things instead of the few low totem pole jobs patronage offered. John F. Kennedy had won the 1960 presidential election only with the vote, mostly solid in the south, from Negro voters. In South Carolina, Negroes had turned down patronage offers of the Truman administration when he was continued as president in 1948. Two years later, they had also rejected patronage slots from incumbent U.S. Senator Olin D. Johnson, who narrowly defeated former Governor J. Strom Thurmond. The only thing new then in 1961 in the request filed with the Democratic National Committee was it now included 11 states - instead of only South Carolina.
One of the most vibrant persons in the June 1962 organizational meeting was YMCA Secretary Warren Cochrane, a native of Charleston. It is interesting to recall that some 22 years later, what both Mr. Cochrane and Georgia s first post-Reconstruction Black senator- to-be, Attorney LeRoy Johnson, argued is very much a reality in 1984: they urged for programs within the new Democratic (Southern) Conference that insured against Negroes in the 11 member states being exploited by persons of their own ethnic group living outside the south. It was a heated meeting and recessed - not adjourned - to a September meeting in Birmingham.
SOME THINK AREA PEOPLE DUMB
The National Committee sent down from Washington Deputy Chairman Louis E. Martin and White House staffer Andrew Hatcher for the June 1962 meeting. The Deputy Chairman reported funds had been contributed by a foundation to launch registration. The money had been allocated among three groups, NAACP, Southern Regional Council and the fledgling SCLC. No contact nor consultation with the leaders who actually had the voters had been made prior to the session. Nevertheless, the 11 state leaders were the people who rounded up and gotten out the votes Mr. Kennedy won with, doing so out of their own pockets, or money their organizations raised from among Negroes themselves.

Mr. Kennedy s campaign in 1960 was run by a committee that included about six Negroes in key spots. The six lived in, and north of, Washington, D.C., Marjorie Mackenzie Lawson apparently the most influential. Robert F. Kennedy, the candidate s brother, ran the campaign and indications were to turn up that he had been led to believe the six Blacks referred to were the nation s Negro brokers; that the rank and file Negro would follow them blindly. This was a New Frontiers campaign, and as literal as the words implied - younger and more sophisticated people, including six hand-picked Blacks. By August, Bobby Kennedy and the New Frontier people were stunned. The six people they d picked really didn t have the influence, impact and pull at first thought. But RFK et al did a fast about face. They feld to Dawson, apologized and urged him to help save the November election for the party. And to whom did Dawson turned? To the small 11 state leaders who established the Southern Democratic Conference two years later.

Negro voters in this area, inspite of what one reads and hears or sees via media reports, have increased only because of efforts of local people living and working among them. These local people are given no recognition or credit today, just as none was given those ahead of them 22 years ago. We ve even had instances this year where outsiders have come into the area and attempted to discredit our own people who dare to think for themselves, who have been elected by people in their communities and insist on serving their communities rather than hand over everything they have built up to outsiders whose principle interest is self-deification and patronage and money.
The Southern Democratic Conference was intended to deal with things like what we re talking about. In 1962 and around that time they were kept out of, say South Carolina, and some other states. The reasoning then was if the Negro in the South is to become free, he must do it mostly himself. All he can get from most Negroes outside the area is a lot of mouth, a lot of collection plates - both before him and before others who are told he will benefit from the collections. A recounting of changes in the lifestyle of the south indisputably shows the southern Negro had had the courage, the determination and ability to organize his community behind goals he sets. He doesn t get, and really doesn t need, outside help. That is exactly what William Patterson proposed to S.C. Progressive Democrats in 1944. Aw, he beamed, they had done a marvelous, unbelievable thing. But they needed to have outside help which, in that case, was being offered by Communists. Asked where had he and his people been all the years Negro South Carolinians had wallowed in misery and deprivation? The man flushed in anger, swearing and accusing the party of being blankety blank nationalists.
